fields.title: Kedr: Revenue Grows, Cash Shrinks
fields.summary: More clients, thinner bank account. Decide what to do with the model.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do with an eight-month runway?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Kedr.
fields.brief/company: Kedr is a fictional cloud warehouse management service for small distributors. 120 clients, average check of 40 thousand rubles per month.
fields.brief/context: Over the year, clients grew by 34%, revenue increased by 31%, but there is less cash in the account than a year ago. The CFO says that at the current rate, the money will last for eight months. The board demands faster growth.
fields.brief/objective: Understand the economics and decide what to change.
fields.brief/constraints: Eight-month runway. A team of 14 people, a sales team of three.
fields.brief/task: Choose a solution and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Growing revenue and growing cash are not the same thing
fields.learnTakeaway/body: If customer costs are paid upfront while revenue comes in monthly, rapid growth accelerates cash depletion. This is a cash flow gap, cured by shifting the payment timing. At the same time, check the contribution by segment: the database average almost always hides a group you serve at a loss. The first free cure here is disqualification criteria for sales.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Reserves: 16.8 million ₽. Burn rate: 2.1 million ₽ per month above revenue. Runway — 8 months.

Implementation (60,000 ₽) and acquisition (180,000 ₽) are paid at the time of the deal, while the customer pays monthly: each new customer initially drains cash and only starts returning it from the sixth month.

Payment: monthly for 96% of customers. Almost no annual prepayments: no annual discount was offered.

Two large contracts are planned for next quarter, but neither is signed.

Prices haven't been raised for three years.

If growth stops, the company breaks even in about three months.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Board: 'accelerate growth, hire two more salespeople'.

CCO: take everyone who pays, including retail chains and manufacturing — 'revenue is revenue'.

CFO asks for at least an annual prepayment with a discount.

One of the PMs suggests a direction for manufacturing companies: estimated payback period of 14 months.

Development asks for three months to cut infrastructure costs in half.

Support is overloaded: 12 retail chains generate more than half of the tickets.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
From September 1, mandatory labeling is required for two more product groups: this affects 40% of our customer base and most potential clients. We don't have it, estimate is 8 weeks.

Our competitor has labeling, but only in their expensive tier.

Raising prices by 15%: market experience shows that 3–6% churn with such an increase; it would become unprofitable only with churn above 13%.

Retail chains with a 60% price increase: four will likely leave, the rest will become profitable.

Our implementation time is 3.4 days compared to two weeks for a major competitor.

Sales currently rejects no one: there are no disqualification criteria.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Fix economics by segment and payment timing
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Stop acquiring unprofitable segments, reprice retail chains, raise prices, shift payments closer to the time of expenses, and direct development to labeling.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
A segment analysis explains the paradox: revenue is growing because there are more clients, but cash is burning because 14 out of 41 new ones are retail chains and manufacturers with a negative contribution, and each new client initially costs 240 thousand.
You give sales rejection criteria: we don't take manufacturers, and chains only at the new price. This is the first thing that stops burning cash.
You raise the price for chains by 60%: four leave, eight become profitable, and support workload is cut in half.
You raise the price for new clients by 15% — it would become unprofitable with churn above 13%, while 3–6% is expected.
You introduce an annual prepayment with a 10% discount: 28 clients switch to it within a quarter, closing the cash gap faster than any cost-cutting.
You send development to work on labeling: 8 weeks, deadline September 1, 40% of the customer base must upgrade.
After two quarters, the burn rate drops from 2.1 million to 0.4 million, and the runway is over two years.
Compromise: the number of clients barely grows, and you had to explain to the board why this was the right move.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The board is right: growth is needed. Hire two salespeople and take everyone who is ready to pay.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Sales increase, revenue grows faster — and cash runs out faster too.
Each new client costs 240 thousand at the time of the deal and only pays it back starting from the sixth month, while some new ones — retail chains and manufacturers — never pay it back at all.
The burn rate increases from 2.1 to 3.4 million per month, and the runway shrinks from eight months to five.
Two pending contracts factored into the plan are not signed on time.
By the sixth month, expenses must be cut urgently, and development is the first to go — along with labeling, which is mandatory from September 1.
Compromise: you accelerated the growth that was causing the cash to disappear in the first place.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Development promises to cut infrastructure costs in half in three months. This will reduce variable costs per customer.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The work is done and yields results: infrastructure costs drop from 3,000 to 1,500 ₽ per customer per month.
At scale, this is 2.2 million per year — nice, but significantly less than needed: the burn rate is 2.1 million per month.
Three months of development with an eight-month runway are spent on an item that makes up a small part of variable costs; retail chain support costs four times more and remains untouched.
Labeling is not released by September 1.
Trade-off: the cost cut was chosen for its ease, not its size; it does not affect the main source of expenses — payment timing and unprofitable segments.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The CFO is right: monthly payments with upfront acquisition costs create a gap. Offer a year with a discount.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The measure hits the cash flow gap directly: 28 clients switch to annual billing in a quarter, and cash comes in earlier.
Runway grows from eight months to thirteen — the fastest improvement available.
But unprofitable segments remain: retail chains with negative contribution and manufacturing with a five-month lifetime keep coming because sales has no disqualification criteria.
Prepayment makes their harm less noticeable: money comes upfront, but the contribution is still negative.
By the end of the year, the customer base structure worsens, even though the bank account looks better.
Trade-off: the right cure for a cash flow gap, used instead of treating unprofitable segments.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Economics are calculated for the whole company, not per customer and by segment
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The decision was made without considering reserves, burn rate, and runway
